construct: Nonrival consumption and vertical summation of marginal benefits
why: The stem supplies the common public-good quantity, the fact that benefits are summed vertically, or the omitted group's positive marginal benefit. The general summation/nonrivalry principle resolves the question.
repair: Require one or both groups' benefit readings at a plotted quantity and retain the justification for summing benefits rather than quantities. Pair actual values with a wrong aggregation rule and provide two plausible correctly aggregated values.

construct: Efficient public-good provision using aggregate marginal benefits
why: Only the key sums both beneficiaries at a common quantity and compares the result with MC. Other choices substitute one group, add quantities, average valuations, or deny that an added beneficiary can affect the optimum.
repair: Include two correctly aggregated marginal-benefit or efficient-quantity candidates differing in graph readings; retain the actual readings under an incorrect single-group or horizontal-addition interpretation.

construct: Monopoly marginal revenue, profit maximization, natural monopoly and average-cost pricing
why: The stem asks why monopoly MR is below price, why moving beyond the maximizing quantity loses profit, what characterizes natural monopoly, or why fair-return pricing breaks even. The generic economic condition identifies the answer.
repair: Require the plotted MR/MC relationship or regulated price/ATC at a particular output and apply the same economic explanation. Do not state the optimizing or break-even conclusion before asking students to infer it.
